questions.question_text:
A parcel is delivered on time with probability $0.91$.
One parcel is chosen at random and $X=1$ if it is delivered on time.
Which model and mean are correct?

options.why: Used the late rate as $p$, although the question defines an on-time delivery as the success.
Gave the variance $p(1-p)$ in place of the mean $p$.
Used the late rate as $p$ and also reported the variance instead of the mean.

questions.solution_text:
Success: the parcel is delivered on time.
$p=0.91$
$X \sim \text{Bernoulli}(0.91)$
$E(X)=0.91$

questions.question_text:
In a town $46\%$ of adults hold a library card.
One adult is chosen at random and $X=1$ if that adult holds a card.
Find $\text{Var}(X)$.

options.why: Gave the mean $p$ instead of the variance $p(1-p)$.
Gave the probability of failure $1-p$ instead of the variance.
Computed $p^2$ instead of $p(1-p)$.

questions.question_text:
A dart player hits the bullseye with probability $0.2$ on each independent throw.
Find the probability that she misses the first throw and hits the second.

options.why: Multiplied $0.2 \times 0.2$, treating both throws as hits.
Multiplied $0.8 \times 0.8$, treating both throws as misses.
Gave only the probability of hitting the second throw, ignoring the first throw.

questions.question_text:
A Bernoulli variable has $X=1$ when a randomly chosen commuter cycles to work, and $E(X)=0.18$.
What does this value mean?

options.text: In the long run, $18\%$ of randomly chosen commuters cycle to work.
$0.18$ commuters cycle to work each day.
options.why: Reads the mean as a count of people rather than a proportion for one trial.

options.text: A randomly chosen commuter cycles $0.18$ of the way to work.
options.why: Treats the mean as a distance rather than a long-run proportion of successes.

options.text: The most likely value of $X$ is $0.18$.
options.why: The mean is not a value $X$ can take, since $X$ is only ever $0$ or $1$.

questions.solution_text:
$E(X)=p$
$=0.18$
For a Bernoulli variable the mean is the probability of success, which is the long-run proportion of commuters who cycle to work.

questions.question_text:
A student writes $X \sim \text{Bernoulli}(0.3)$ for '$X$ is the number of sixes in $20$ rolls of a die'.
Which statement identifies the error?

options.text: $X$ counts successes over $20$ trials, so it is not a single-trial Bernoulli variable.
The probability should be $\frac{1}{6}$, but the model is otherwise correct.
options.why: Corrects the probability but leaves the fatal error that $X$ counts results over many rolls.

options.text: A die has six faces, so no Bernoulli model can describe rolling a die.
options.why: Recording only whether a roll shows a six does give exactly two outcomes, so a Bernoulli model is possible.

options.text: The rolls are not independent, so no model applies.
options.why: Separate rolls of a die are independent; independence is not what is wrong here.

questions.solution_text:
A Bernoulli random variable describes exactly one trial and takes only the values $0$ and $1$.
Counting sixes over $20$ rolls gives a variable that can take the values $0$ to $20$, so the model is wrong.
A correct Bernoulli model uses one roll, with $X=1$ if that roll shows a six.

questions.question_text:
A smoke alarm passes its monthly test with probability $0.97$, independently each month.
Find the probability that it passes in each of the first two months and fails in the third, correct to four decimal places.

options.why: Used only two months, multiplying $0.97 \times 0.03$ and ignoring the second pass.
Found the probability of three passes, $0.97^3$, instead of two passes and a failure.
Multiplied three failure probabilities, $0.03^3$, instead of two passes and one failure.

questions.question_text:
A Bernoulli variable records whether a randomly chosen tyre is under-inflated.
Its variance is $0.2275$ and fewer than half of all tyres are under-inflated.
Find $p$.

options.why: Chose the root above $0.5$, against the condition that fewer than half are under-inflated.
Took the square root of the variance, which gives the standard deviation, not $p$.
Halved the variance instead of solving $p(1-p)=0.2275$.

questions.solution_text:
$p(1-p)=0.2275$
$p^2-p+0.2275=0$
$p=\frac{1 \pm \sqrt{1-0.91}}{2}$
$=\frac{1 \pm 0.3}{2}$
$p=0.65$ or $p=0.35$
Fewer than half are under-inflated, so $p=0.35$

questions.question_text:
A vaccine works for a randomly chosen person with probability $p$, independently.
For one person the Bernoulli variable has $\text{Var}(X)=0.0564$, and the vaccine works for most people, so $p>0.5$.
Find the probability that the vaccine works for two consecutive people.

options.why: Used the root below $0.5$, $p=0.06$, and squared it.
Doubled the variance instead of squaring $p$.
Stopped at $p$ without finding the probability for two people.
